items.title: Nature of Indian Federalism, Territory & Reorganisation (Art 1-4)
items.body:
## In one line

India is a **Union of States** — a federation with a strong Centre, where the Union itself can redraw State boundaries.

## Why it is asked

The exact wording of Article 1, the 'quasi-federal' label, and the Article 2 vs Article 3 difference are classic one-mark and statement questions.

## The story

**Article 1** declares that 'India, that is Bharat, shall be a **Union of States**'. Dr Ambedkar explained the phrase carefully: the Indian federation is **not based on an agreement** between states, and **no state has the right to secede** (break away). He called it an **indestructible union of destructible states** — the Centre can reshape states, but states can never leave.

Because so much power leans towards the Centre — a single citizenship, a single integrated judiciary, all-India services, one Constitution and strong emergency powers — scholars say Indian federalism is **'federal in form but unitary in spirit'**. K. C. Wheare famously called it **quasi-federal** ('quasi' means 'almost' or 'partly').

Articles 2-4 give the Union the power to reorganise the map:

| Article | Content |
|---|---|
| 2 | Admission or establishment of **new states** into the Union (for example Sikkim, 1975) |
| 3 | Forming new states, or altering areas, boundaries or names from **existing** territory |
| 4 | Such laws are **not** amendments under Article 368; they pass by a **simple majority** |

A bill under Article 3 needs the **prior recommendation of the President**, and the affected state legislature must be **consulted** — but its view is **not binding** on Parliament. Major reorganisations include **Andhra (1953)**, India's first linguistic state (created after Potti Sriramulu's fast and death), the **States Reorganisation Act 1956** (14 states + 6 Union Territories), **Telangana (2014)** and the **J&K and Ladakh Union Territories (2019)**.

## Why it matters

This is the constitutional basis for how India's political map keeps changing — and why a state cannot resist being reorganised.

## Terms explained

- **Secede** — to formally withdraw from the Union; Indian states cannot.
- **Quasi-federal** — partly federal; a federation with a strong central tilt.
- **Simple majority** — more than half of the members present and voting (an ordinary vote).
- **Linguistic state** — a state formed on the basis of a common language.

## Don't confuse

| Article | Deals with |
|---|---|
| Article 2 | New states coming in from **outside** the Union |
| Article 3 | New states carved from **existing** Indian territory |

## Remember it

Articles 1-4 in order: **'1 defines, 2 admits, 3 alters, 4 clarifies (not an amendment).'**

## TL;DR

- Article 1 calls India a 'Union of States' — an indestructible union with no right of secession.
- Indian federalism is quasi-federal: federal in form, unitary in spirit (strong Centre, single citizenship).
- Article 2 = admission of new states; Article 3 = internal reorganisation from existing territory.
- An Article 3 bill needs prior presidential recommendation; the state legislature is consulted but not bound.
- Article 4 makes reorganisation laws non-amendments, passed by simple majority; SRA 1956 created 14 states and 6 UTs.
keyPoints: Article 1 calls India a 'Union of States' — an indestructible union with no right of secession.
Indian federalism is quasi-federal: federal in form, unitary in spirit (strong Centre, single citizenship).
Art 2 = admission of new states; Art 3 = internal reorganisation from existing territory.
Art 3 bill needs prior presidential recommendation; state legislature is consulted but not bound.
Art 4 makes reorganisation laws non-amendments, passed by simple majority.
States Reorganisation Act 1956 created 14 states and 6 UTs on linguistic lines.
items.mnemonic: Articles 1-4 order: '1 defines, 2 admits, 3 alters, 4 clarifies (not an amendment).'
items.source: Constitution of India, Articles 1-4; APPSC GK PDF — Union and its Territory

items.title: Legislative Relations & the Seventh Schedule
items.body:
## In one line

The **Seventh Schedule** splits law-making subjects into three lists — Union, State and Concurrent — and the Centre keeps the upper hand.

## Why it is asked

The subject counts, who holds residuary powers, and the five ways Parliament can enter the State List are heavily tested.

## The story

Law-making is divided by territory and by subject. Under **Article 245**, Parliament can make laws for the whole or any part of India, and a state legislature for its own territory. The **Seventh Schedule** then divides subjects into three lists:

| List | Original → present subjects | Who legislates |
|---|---|---|
| Union | 97 → 100 | Parliament |
| State | 66 → 61 | State legislature |
| Concurrent | 47 → 52 | Both (Union prevails) |

Anything not on any list — the **residuary powers** (Article 248), including residuary taxation — belongs to **Parliament** (an idea borrowed from Canada). This is a clear centralising feature.

Even on the State List, Parliament can step in by five routes:

| Article | When Parliament may legislate on the State List |
|---|---|
| 249 | Rajya Sabha passes a two-thirds resolution in the national interest |
| 250 | A National Emergency is in operation |
| 252 | Two or more states request it |
| 253 | To implement an international treaty or agreement |
| 356 | During President's Rule in a state |

When a State law clashes with a Union law on a **Concurrent** subject, **Article 254** says the **Union law prevails** (this clash is called **repugnancy**). The one exception: if the State law was reserved for and received the **President's assent**, it prevails in that state — though Parliament can still override it later.

## Why it matters

This is the engine room of federalism — it decides who can make which law, and why the Centre usually wins a clash.

## Terms explained

- **Residuary powers** — authority over subjects not listed anywhere; held by Parliament.
- **Concurrent subject** — a topic on which both the Union and states can legislate.
- **Repugnancy** — a direct conflict between a Union law and a State law on the same subject.
- **Presidential assent** — the President's approval of a reserved State bill.

## Don't confuse

| Point | Position |
|---|---|
| Residuary powers | With Parliament (not the states) |
| Clash on Concurrent List | Union law prevails (Article 254) |

## Remember it

State-List entry Articles **'249-250-252-253'** = **interest, emergency, request, treaty**.

## TL;DR

- Seventh Schedule: Union List (100), State List (61), Concurrent List (52) subjects.
- Residuary powers of legislation and taxation vest in Parliament under Article 248.
- Parliament can legislate on the State List via Articles 249, 250, 252, 253 and during Article 356.
- Article 254: a Union law prevails over a repugnant State law on Concurrent subjects.
- A repugnant State law with presidential assent prevails in that state, subject to parliamentary override.
keyPoints: Seventh Schedule: Union List (100), State List (61), Concurrent List (52) subjects.
Residuary powers of legislation and taxation vest in Parliament under Article 248.
Parliament can legislate on State List via Articles 249, 250, 252, 253 and during Art 356.
Article 254: Union law prevails over a repugnant state law on Concurrent subjects.
A repugnant state law with presidential assent prevails in that state, subject to parliamentary override.
items.mnemonic: State-List override Articles '249-250-252-253' = interest, emergency, request, treaty.
items.source: Constitution of India, Articles 245-255 & Seventh Schedule

items.title: Administrative Relations & Coordination Machinery
items.body:
## In one line

The Centre can direct states on key matters, shares the all-India services with them, and runs councils to smooth cooperation.

## Why it is asked

The directive Articles (256-257), the all-India services (312) and the Inter-State Council (263) recur in statement-based questions.

## The story

Administrative relations run through **Articles 256-263**. **Article 256** requires every state to ensure **compliance with Union laws**. **Article 257** says a state's executive power must **not impede** the Union's, and lets the Union direct states on **communications and railways of national importance**. **Article 261** requires 'full faith and credit' to be given to the public acts, records and judicial proceedings of the Union and of every state.

A powerful unifying device is the **All-India Services** (IAS, IPS, Indian Forest Service) under **Article 312**: these officers serve **both** the Union and the states, and creating a new All-India Service needs a Rajya Sabha resolution. Because the Centre controls recruitment and discipline at the top, this is a strong centralising feature.

To smooth cooperation, two kinds of bodies exist. The **Inter-State Council (Article 263)** is a **recommendatory** body set up in **1990** on the advice of the **Sarkaria Commission**; it is chaired by the Prime Minister with Chief Ministers and select Union ministers. **Zonal Councils** are **statutory** bodies created under the States Reorganisation Act 1956 (five zones, plus the separate North-Eastern Council) to promote inter-state cooperation.

## Why it matters

These provisions keep administration coordinated across 28 states and 8 Union Territories, and explain why IAS/IPS officers answer to both levels.

## Terms explained

- **Executive power** — the power to carry out and enforce laws.
- **All-India Services** — services common to the Union and states (IAS, IPS, IFoS) under Article 312.
- **Recommendatory body** — one that advises; its suggestions are not binding.
- **Statutory body** — a body created by an Act of Parliament (not by the Constitution).

## Don't confuse

| Body | Nature |
|---|---|
| Inter-State Council (Art 263) | Constitutional, recommendatory |
| Zonal Councils | Statutory (SRA 1956), not constitutional |

## Remember it

**'256 comply, 257 don't impede, 263 council, 312 services.'**

## TL;DR

- Articles 256-257: states must comply with Union laws and not impede Union executive power.
- Article 257 lets the Union direct states on communications and railways of national importance.
- All-India Services (Article 312) are common to the Union and states — a centralising feature.
- Inter-State Council (Article 263) set up in 1990 on Sarkaria's recommendation; PM-chaired, recommendatory.
- Zonal Councils are statutory bodies under the States Reorganisation Act 1956.
keyPoints: Art 256-257: states must comply with Union laws and not impede Union executive power.
Art 257 lets the Union direct states on communications/railways of national importance.
All-India Services (Art 312) are common to Union and states — a centralising feature.
Inter-State Council (Art 263) set up in 1990 on Sarkaria's recommendation; PM-chaired, recommendatory.
Zonal Councils are statutory bodies under the States Reorganisation Act 1956.
items.source: Constitution of India, Articles 256-263 & 312; Sarkaria Commission Report

items.title: Financial Relations, Finance Commission & GST Council
items.body:
## In one line

The Centre collects the big taxes and shares them with states through the **Finance Commission**, while the **GST Council** jointly sets GST.

## Why it is asked

The Finance Commission's Article and cycle, the current (16th) commission, and the GST Council's voting rule are frequent current-plus-static questions.

## The story

Taxes are divided between the Union and the states under **Articles 268-293** — for example, the Union taxes income **but not agricultural income**, which is a State subject. Because states spend more than they can raise, the Centre transfers money to them in two ways: **statutory grants-in-aid** under **Article 275** (on the Finance Commission's advice) and **discretionary grants** under **Article 282**.

The **Finance Commission (Article 280)** is a **quasi-judicial constitutional body** that the President constitutes **every fifth year**, with a **chairman and four members**. It recommends: (i) the **vertical** split of the shared tax pool between the Centre and states, (ii) the **horizontal** split among the states, (iii) the principles for grants-in-aid, and (iv) measures to boost state funds for panchayats and municipalities.

| Finance Commission | Chairman | Award period |
|---|---|---|
| 14th | Y. V. Reddy | 2015-20 |
| 15th | N. K. Singh | 2020-26 |
| 16th | Arvind Panagariya | 2026-31 |

The **Sixteenth Finance Commission** (constituted December 2023) is chaired by **Arvind Panagariya**; its recommendations cover **1 April 2026 to 31 March 2031**.

The **GST Council (Article 279A)** was added by the **101st Amendment Act, 2016**. It is chaired by the **Union Finance Minister**, with state finance ministers as members. In voting, the **Centre holds one-third of the votes and the states together two-thirds**, and every decision needs a **three-fourths majority** — a design often called **cooperative fiscal federalism** or **'pooled sovereignty'**, because neither side can decide alone.

## Why it matters

This machinery decides how much money each state actually gets — the practical heart of fiscal federalism and a live political issue.

## Terms explained

- **Quasi-judicial body** — a body that decides matters in a court-like, impartial way.
- **Vertical devolution** — the share of taxes passing from the Centre down to the states as a group.
- **Horizontal devolution** — how that states' share is divided among individual states.
- **Grants-in-aid** — financial help given by the Centre to states.
- **Pooled sovereignty** — Centre and states exercising a power jointly, neither alone.

## Don't confuse

| Body | Article | Chair |
|---|---|---|
| Finance Commission | 280 | Appointed chairman (now Panagariya) |
| GST Council | 279A | Union Finance Minister |

## Remember it

Finance Commission chairs: **'14-Reddy, 15-Singh, 16-Panagariya'** → periods step 2015, 2020, 2026.

## TL;DR

- Finance Commission is constituted under Article 280 every five years — chairman + 4 members.
- Statutory grants-in-aid = Article 275; discretionary grants = Article 282.
- 16th Finance Commission: chair Arvind Panagariya, award period 2026-31 (constituted December 2023).
- GST Council (Article 279A, 101st Amendment 2016): Centre 1/3 votes, states 2/3, decisions need a 3/4 majority.
- The Union taxes income excluding agricultural income, which is a State List subject.

items.title: Commissions on Centre-State Relations & Dispute Machinery
items.body:
## In one line

Three commissions reviewed how the Centre and states should share power, and the Constitution provides special machinery for President's Rule and water disputes.

## Why it is asked

Matching each commission to its year and sponsor, and the Bommai case on Article 356, are frequent exam points.

## The story

Three bodies examined Centre-State relations:

| Body | Year | Set up by | Focus |
|---|---|---|---|
| Rajamannar Committee | 1969 | Tamil Nadu govt | State autonomy; less central control |
| Sarkaria Commission | 1983-88 | Centre (R. S. Sarkaria) | Centre-State relations |
| Punchhi Commission | 2007-10 | Centre (M. M. Punchhi) | Centre-State relations (post-liberalisation) |

Their **common recommendations** were: use **Article 356** sparingly, as a last resort; give states a **consultative role** in appointing Governors; strengthen the **Inter-State Council**; and keep the Governor a detached, apolitical figure. Sarkaria opposed abolishing Article 356 but wanted it a genuine last resort; Punchhi suggested a **fixed five-year tenure** for Governors and **'localising emergencies'** to the troubled districts rather than a whole state.

Two special dispute mechanisms matter. **President's Rule (Article 356)** was frequently misused until **S. R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994)**, where the Supreme Court made the proclamation **judicially reviewable**, insisted the majority be proved by a **floor test** in the Assembly (not the Governor's opinion), and affirmed **secularism and federalism** as basic features. For **inter-state water disputes**, **Article 262** lets Parliament set up tribunals and even **bar the jurisdiction of all courts, including the Supreme Court**; this is given effect by the **Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956** and the **River Boards Act, 1956**.

## Why it matters

These reports and the Bommai ruling are the main checks that stopped the Centre from casually dismissing state governments.

## Terms explained

- **State autonomy** — a state's freedom to govern its own affairs with less central control.
- **President's Rule (Article 356)** — central takeover of a state when its constitutional machinery fails.
- **Floor test** — a vote on the Assembly floor to prove a government's majority.
- **Water-disputes tribunal** — a special body (not an ordinary court) that decides river-sharing disputes.

## Don't confuse

| Commission | Year | Set up by |
|---|---|---|
| Rajamannar | 1969 | Tamil Nadu government |
| Sarkaria | 1983-88 | Centre |
| Punchhi | 2007-10 | Centre |

## Remember it

**'Bommai = floor test + judicial review of Article 356'**; **'262 = water, courts barred.'**

## TL;DR

- Rajamannar Committee (1969, Tamil Nadu) championed state autonomy and less central control.
- Sarkaria Commission (1983-88) and Punchhi Commission (2007-10) reviewed Centre-State relations.
- Common recommendation: use Article 356 as a last resort and consult states on Governor appointments.
- S. R. Bommai (1994): the Article 356 proclamation is judicially reviewable; majority tested on the floor of the House.
- Article 262 lets Parliament set up water-dispute tribunals and exclude court jurisdiction; the two 1956 Acts give effect to it.
keyPoints: Rajamannar Committee (1969, Tamil Nadu) championed state autonomy and less central control.
Sarkaria Commission (1983-88) and Punchhi Commission (2007-10) reviewed Centre-State relations.

S. R. Bommai (1994): Art 356 proclamation is judicially reviewable; majority tested on the floor of the House.
Article 262 lets Parliament set up water-dispute tribunals and exclude court jurisdiction.
Inter-State River Water Disputes Act and River Boards Act were both enacted in 1956.
items.source: Sarkaria & Punchhi Commission Reports; Rajamannar Committee Report; S. R. Bommai (1994)

items.title: Union Territories & Trends in Federalism
items.body:
## In one line

Union Territories are run by the Centre through administrators, and modern federalism is moving towards cooperation and competition between the Centre and states.

## Why it is asked

The NCT Delhi arrangement (69th Amendment) and the cooperative-versus-competitive-federalism institutions are current favourites.

## The story

**Union Territories (Articles 239-241)** are administered by the **President through administrators** (Article 239), who are titled **Lieutenant Governor** or **Administrator**. Most UTs have no legislature, but **Puducherry** and the **National Capital Territory (NCT) of Delhi** have their own **legislative assemblies** and councils of ministers with limited powers. The **69th Amendment Act, 1991** gave Delhi its special NCT status; however, **land, police and public order** stay with the Centre through the Lieutenant Governor, which has caused repeated Centre-Delhi friction that the Supreme Court has had to settle more than once.

Federal practice today runs along two trends. **Cooperative federalism** means the Centre and states working together — through the **GST Council**, the **Inter-State Council**, and **NITI Aayog** (which replaced the Planning Commission in 2015 as a shared policy platform). **Competitive federalism** means states competing on outcomes and rankings — such as the Ease of Doing Business index and the Aspirational Districts programme — to attract investment. The economic liberalisation after 1991 enlarged the states' economic role and deepened both trends.

## Why it matters

It explains both the special, friction-prone status of Delhi and the modern, more partnership-based direction of Indian federalism.

## Terms explained

- **Union Territory** — a region governed directly by the Centre, not a full state.
- **Lieutenant Governor** — the Centre's appointed administrator of certain UTs.
- **NCT of Delhi** — National Capital Territory of Delhi, a special UT with an assembly.
- **Cooperative federalism** — Centre and states working jointly on shared goals.
- **Competitive federalism** — states competing with one another to perform better.

## Don't confuse

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Cooperative federalism | Centre and states collaborate (GST Council, NITI Aayog) |
| Competitive federalism | States compete on rankings and investment |

## Remember it

**'Delhi = assembly but land-police-order with the Centre (69th Amendment, 1991).'**

## TL;DR

- UTs are administered by the President through administrators / Lieutenant Governors (Article 239).
- Puducherry and NCT Delhi have legislative assemblies with limited powers.
- 69th Amendment (1991) gave Delhi NCT status; land, police and public order remain with the Centre.
- Cooperative-federalism institutions: GST Council, Inter-State Council, NITI Aayog (2015).
- Competitive federalism: states compete via rankings like Ease of Doing Business and Aspirational Districts.
keyPoints: UTs are administered by the President through administrators/Lieutenant Governors (Art 239).
Puducherry and NCT Delhi have legislative assemblies with limited powers.
69th Amendment (1991) gave Delhi NCT status; land, police, public order remain with the Centre.
Cooperative federalism institutions: GST Council, Inter-State Council, NITI Aayog (2015).
Competitive federalism: states compete via rankings like Ease of Doing Business and Aspirational Districts.
items.source: Constitution of India, Articles 239-241; APPSC GK PDF — Union and its Territory; NITI Aayog

items.title: Fifth/Sixth Schedules & Extra-constitutional Bodies
items.body:
## In one line

The Fifth and Sixth Schedules protect tribal areas, and some well-known bodies (Planning Commission, NDC) were never part of the Constitution at all.

## Why it is asked

The exact four Sixth-Schedule states and the 'not in the Constitution' trap are common one-mark questions.

## The story

The **Fifth Schedule** provides for the administration of **Scheduled Areas** in most states and specifically protects **tribal land from being transferred to non-tribals**. The **Sixth Schedule** goes further for the north-east: it creates **autonomous district and regional councils** for the tribal areas of **Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram**, giving them real law-making and administrative powers. Both schedules exist to protect the Scheduled Tribes.

Some bodies people assume are constitutional are not. The **Planning Commission** and the **National Development Council (NDC)** were **not mentioned in the Constitution** and were **non-statutory** executive bodies (the Planning Commission was replaced by NITI Aayog in 2015). By contrast, **Zonal Councils** are **statutory** — created by the States Reorganisation Act 1956 — but still not constitutional. Keeping these categories straight (constitutional / statutory / extra-constitutional) is the whole point of the question.

## Why it matters

Tribal-area protection is a live governance and rights issue, and the 'what is not in the Constitution' distinction is a classic examiner trap.

## Terms explained

- **Scheduled Area** — a tribal-majority area given special protection under the Fifth Schedule.
- **Autonomous council** — an elected tribal body with limited self-government (Sixth Schedule).
- **Non-statutory / extra-constitutional** — created by executive decision, with no Act or Constitution backing it.
- **Statutory** — created by an Act of Parliament.

## Don't confuse

| Body | Status |
|---|---|
| Finance / Inter-State / GST Councils | Constitutional |
| Zonal Councils | Statutory (SRA 1956) |
| Planning Commission, NDC | Extra-constitutional, non-statutory |

## Remember it

Sixth Schedule states = **'A-M-T-M'**: **A**ssam, **M**eghalaya, **T**ripura, **M**izoram.

## TL;DR

- Fifth Schedule administers Scheduled Areas and bars transfer of tribal land to non-tribals.
- Sixth Schedule gives autonomous councils to the tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.
- The Planning Commission and NDC were extra-constitutional and non-statutory.
- Zonal Councils are statutory (States Reorganisation Act 1956), not constitutional.
- Finance, Inter-State and GST Councils are the constitutional bodies — do not mix the categories.
keyPoints: Fifth Schedule administers Scheduled Areas and bars transfer of tribal land to non-tribals.
Sixth Schedule gives autonomous councils to tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.
The Planning Commission and NDC were extra-constitutional and non-statutory; Zonal Councils are statutory, not constitutional.

items.title: For Mains — Union-State Relations & Federalism
items.body:
The federalism clauses in **GS Paper-3 (mains-3)** — 'Federal structure, role of Governor, distribution of powers (lists)' and the law clause on Centre-State lists — reward an analytical, balanced answer that weighs centralising features against counter-trends.

| Dimension | Content to deploy |
|---|---|
| Nature | 'Union of States' (Art 1); Wheare's quasi-federal; indestructible union |
| Centralising features | Residuary powers (248), Art 254 supremacy, Arts 249-253, all-India services (312), emergency (352/356/360) |
| Federal safeguards | Written supreme Constitution, independent judiciary, bicameral Parliament, Art 3 state consultation |
| Fiscal federalism | Finance Commission (280), GST Council (279A), vertical/horizontal devolution, cesses debate |
| Role of Governor | Centre's appointee; discretion in Art 356, bill reservation, CM appointment — reform demands |
| Counter-trends | Cooperative federalism (GST Council, NITI Aayog, Inter-State Council), competitive federalism, coalition era |

**Data points, committees and judgments to quote:** *S. R. Bommai* (1994) — Article 356 justiciable, floor test, federalism a basic feature; **Sarkaria (1983-88)** and **Punchhi (2007-10)** Commissions on Article 356 and the Governor; **16th Finance Commission** (Arvind Panagariya, award period 2026-31); **GST Council** (101st Amendment, 2016) three-fourths-majority rule; the **Inter-State Council** (1990) and NITI Aayog (2015).

**AP angle:** post-2014 bifurcation left Andhra Pradesh with a revenue gap and a strong stake in Finance Commission devolution and special-assistance demands; inter-state river-water sharing (Krishna, Godavari) with Telangana shows Article 262 federalism in action.

**Use in answers:**
- *Example:* use the GST compensation-delay and cesses-shrinking-the-divisible-pool debate to argue that fiscal autonomy needs strengthening.
- *Quote:* Ambedkar — India is a 'Union of States', 'an indestructible union'.
- *Diagram idea:* a balance-scale showing centralising features on one pan and cooperative-federalism institutions on the other.

Conclude that India is best described as a **cooperative quasi-federation** — a strong Centre for unity, with evolving practice protecting state autonomy.
keyPoints: Frame federalism answers as a balance: centralising features vs federal safeguards and cooperative counter-trends.
Anchor with Bommai (1994), Sarkaria (1983-88), Punchhi (2007-10), 16th FC (Panagariya), GST Council (2016).
Role of Governor and Article 356 reform (fixed tenure, consultation) is a core sub-theme.
Fiscal federalism: Finance Commission (280) + GST Council (279A); flag compensation delays and rising cesses.
AP angle: post-bifurcation revenue gap, Finance Commission dependence, Krishna/Godavari water sharing (Art 262).
Open with the 'Union of States' quote; close by calling India a cooperative quasi-federation.
items.source: Constitution of India; S. R. Bommai (1994); Sarkaria/Punchhi Reports; syllabus-map M3-2 / M3-15a
